questions.question: Java programs that run on Java-enabled servers and handle requests like the servers do are called —
questions.explanation: A servlet is a server-side Java class that runs inside a servlet container (e.g., Tomcat) and processes client requests/responses, extending the server's own request-handling capability -- exactly the behaviour described. Applets (A) are client-side Java programs that run inside a browser, the opposite deployment model. Threads (C) are a unit of concurrent execution, not a request-handling component. Ajax (D) is a client-side browser scripting technique for asynchronous updates, unrelated to server-side Java.

questions.question: A software tool that allows Java-based programs to interact with databases is —
questions.explanation: JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is the standard Java API that lets Java applications connect to, query, and update relational databases through driver implementations. ODBC (A) is Microsoft's earlier, language-neutral C-based database API which Java programs can only reach indirectly through a JDBC-ODBC bridge, not directly. 'Java Connect' (C) and 'JSQL' (D) are not real, recognized Java database APIs -- they are distractors invented to sound plausible.

questions.question: In order to create the basic runtime environment, application development and foundation for other Java applications, ____ is sufficient.
questions.explanation: Core Java (Java SE) supplies the JVM, JRE, and the fundamental class libraries needed for basic runtime execution and standalone application development -- it is the base upon which everything else is built. J2EE (A) is an enterprise extension layered on top of Core Java for large-scale, multi-tier applications, so it is not the minimal foundation being asked about. JavaScript (C) is an unrelated browser scripting language, and Java Servlet (D) is a narrow web-tier API that itself depends on Core Java, not a foundation in its own right.

questions.question: Why can't Java be considered by some people to be a pure Object-Oriented language?

options.D: All data and function must belong to a class

questions.explanation: A purely object-oriented language should treat everything as an object; Java's primitive types (int, char, boolean, etc.) are not objects and do not have methods, which is the standard argument cited for why Java is not 'pure' OOP. (B) is irrelevant -- having a main() entry point is just how execution starts, unrelated to OOP purity. (C) is actually a design choice to avoid the diamond problem, not evidence against OOP purity (Java restores it via interfaces). (D) is in fact evidence FOR strong OOP discipline, not against it, since it enforces encapsulation.

questions.question: The intermediate code generated by the Java compiler, which is platform independent, is called —
questions.explanation: javac compiles .java source into .class files containing bytecode -- a platform-independent instruction set interpreted or JIT-compiled by the JVM on any host, which is exactly what gives Java its 'write once, run anywhere' property. Option (A) 'Intermediate code' is a generic term, not the specific, textbook name Java uses; (B) Assembly code is a low-level, processor-specific representation, the opposite of platform independence; (D) 'Codeword' is not a real programming term and is a pure distractor.

questions.question: A client-side scripting language to manage users' interface interactively is —
questions.explanation: JavaScript executes in the browser (the client) and manipulates the DOM to make pages interactive -- validating forms, responding to clicks, updating content -- without round-tripping to the server for every action. Servlet (A) is server-side Java code, the opposite tier. HTML (C) and XHTML (D) are markup languages that describe static page structure and content; they have no scripting/logic capability of their own to 'manage' interactivity.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes Java Native Interface?

options.A: An interface for Java programs to connect to databases
options.B: An interface that allows Java programs to connect to other native applications and libraries
options.C: A Java system call that is used for executing commands across different types of operating systems
options.D: A Java library that is mainly used for real-time monitoring of websites

questions.explanation: JNI (Java Native Interface) is the framework that lets Java code call into, and be called from, native code written in C/C++ and platform-specific libraries -- used when Java needs to reuse existing native code or access OS-level/hardware features the JVM doesn't expose. (A) describes JDBC, a completely different API for database access. (C) mischaracterizes JNI as an OS-agnostic 'system call', which misunderstands its purpose (it is explicitly platform-specific per native library). (D) is fabricated and unrelated to JNI's actual function.

questions.question: Multiple inheritance in Java can be implemented using —
questions.explanation: Java disallows multiple inheritance of implementation between classes to avoid the diamond problem, but a class can implement any number of interfaces, giving it multiple 'is-a' type relationships -- this is Java's supported route to multiple inheritance. (B) is wrong since a class can extend only one superclass. (C) the 'extends' keyword is single-inheritance-only for classes (it is used for multiple inheritance only among interfaces extending interfaces, not classes). (D) Applets are a GUI deployment mechanism, unrelated to inheritance at all.

questions.question: What is true about threading?

options.A: run() method calls start() method and runs the code
options.C: run() method can be called directly without start() method being called
options.D: start() method creates new thread and calls code written in run() method

questions.explanation: Calling start() on a Thread object asks the JVM to allocate a new call stack and OS thread, which then invokes run() to execute the task concurrently. (A) reverses the relationship -- run() never calls start(). (B) is false because run() by itself does not spawn a thread; it is just an ordinary method body. (C) is misleading: run() CAN be called directly, but doing so executes the code synchronously on the current thread with no new thread created, so it is not the intended, threaded behaviour being tested here -- (D) is the mechanism that actually achieves concurrency.

questions.question: What does the finalize() method do in Java?

options.A: It is called when an object is created.
options.B: It is used to explicitly release resources.
options.C: It is called when an object is no longer reachable.
options.D: It is used to declare a method that cannot be overridden.

questions.explanation: finalize() is a protected Object method the garbage collector invokes on an object just before reclaiming its memory, once the object has become unreachable, giving it a last chance to clean up. (A) describes a constructor's job, the opposite lifecycle point. (B) is wrong because finalize() is invoked implicitly by the GC (at an unpredictable time), not called explicitly by the programmer to release resources -- try-with-resources/close() is the explicit mechanism. (D) describes the 'final' keyword/modifier, an unrelated Java feature that happens to share a similar-sounding name.

questions.question: Which method is used to explicitly terminate a thread in Java?
questions.explanation: In classic Java Thread API terms, Thread.stop() is the method historically documented to forcibly terminate a running thread immediately (it is now deprecated/unsafe in modern practice because it can leave shared objects in an inconsistent state, but it remains the textbook answer to 'which method terminates a thread'). interrupt() (D) is the modern recommended alternative, but it only sets an interrupt flag/requests cooperative stopping -- it does not itself terminate the thread. terminate() (A) and abort() (B) are not real methods on java.lang.Thread; they are plausible-sounding distractors.

questions.question: In JDBC, what is the purpose of the ResultSetMetaData interface?

options.A: It provides metadata about the columns in a ResultSet.
options.B: It provides metadata about the database connection.
options.C: It stores the data of the ResultSet.
options.D: It manages the transaction settings for a query.

questions.explanation: ResultSetMetaData exposes information ABOUT the columns of a ResultSet -- column count, names, SQL data types, nullability, precision -- obtained via resultSet.getMetaData(), useful when column structure is not known in advance. (B) describes DatabaseMetaData, a different interface concerned with the connection/driver/database capabilities. (C) is wrong because the ResultSet object itself, not its metadata interface, holds the actual row data. (D) describes transaction control methods on Connection (commit/rollback/setAutoCommit), unrelated to metadata.

questions.question: How can you send a redirect response to the client from a servlet?
questions.explanation: HttpServletResponse.sendRedirect(url) sends an HTTP 302 status back to the browser with a Location header, causing the client to issue a brand-new request to the given URL -- the standard way to redirect. (A) 'response.forward()' does not exist as a real method. (B) 'request.redirect()' is also not a real API call. (D) RequestDispatcher.forward() performs a server-side forward within the same request (the URL in the browser does not change and it is not a client redirect at all), so it answers a different question than the one asked.

questions.question: Which object in JSP is NOT implicitly available?
questions.explanation: JSP automatically provides nine implicit objects: request, response, pageContext, session, application, out, config, page, and exception -- 'cookie' is not among them. Cookies must be retrieved manually via request.getCookies(), so there is no ready-made implicit 'cookie' object. session (A), config (B), and application (C) are each genuine, standard implicit objects representing the HTTP session, the servlet's ServletConfig, and the shared ServletContext respectively.

questions.question: Which annotation is used to define an EJB component class as a Stateless Session Bean?
questions.explanation: @Stateless (javax.ejb.Stateless) marks a session bean class as stateless, meaning the container can pool and reuse instances across clients since no client-specific conversational state is retained between calls. @Stateful (A) marks the opposite kind of bean, one that does retain per-client state across calls. @EJB (C) is a dependency-injection annotation used to inject a reference to an EJB into another component, not to declare a bean's own type. @Singleton (D) declares a bean of which only one instance exists per application, a third distinct EJB session bean type.

questions.question: What will happen if two threads of the same priority are called to be processed simultaneously?

options.A: Anyone will be executed first lexicographically
options.B: Both of them will be executed simultaneously
options.C: None of them will be executed
options.D: It is dependent on the operating system

questions.explanation: The Java Language Specification does not mandate a specific scheduling order among equal-priority threads; the JVM delegates actual scheduling to the underlying OS thread scheduler (round-robin, time-slicing, or another policy). There is no lexicographic ordering by thread name, and true simultaneous execution is only guaranteed on genuinely parallel cores (not assured), so the only universally correct answer is that behaviour is OS-dependent - this is exactly why Java code must never rely on priority for correctness.

Every Java application starts execution inside a JVM-created thread named 'main'. Calling Thread.currentThread() inside main() therefore returns a reference to that main thread, and printing it shows its name as 'main' via toString() (e.g. 'Thread[main,5,main]'). 'Thread' and 'System' are class names appearing in the code, not the thread's own name property (Thread.getName()), which is why they are wrong distractors.

questions.question: Which JDBC type represents a "single precision" floating point number that supports seven digits of mantissa?
questions.explanation: In the JDBC/SQL type mapping, java.sql.Types.REAL maps to a single-precision floating point value (Java float, about 7 significant decimal digits), while confusingly java.sql.Types.FLOAT actually maps to double precision in JDBC by default, and DOUBLE is explicitly double precision (15-17 digits). INTEGER is a whole-number type with no fractional/mantissa concept at all, so it cannot be the answer. The FLOAT-really-means-double quirk is the classic trap in this question.

questions.question: How many result sets are available with the JDBC 2.0 core API?
questions.explanation: JDBC 2.0 introduced scrollable/updatable result sets via three ResultSet type constants: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY (the original JDBC 1.0 cursor-forward-only behaviour), TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE (scrollable, does not reflect underlying data changes), and TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE (scrollable, reflects changes made by others). That gives exactly three distinct result-set types, ruling out 2, 4 and 5. JDBC 2.0 separately added two concurrency modes (read-only/updatable), a different axis, which can make this recall question easy to misremember.

questions.question: Which case of a session bean obtains the UserTransaction object via the EJBContext using the getUserTransaction() method in EJB transaction management?
questions.explanation: Under Bean-Managed Transaction (BMT) demarcation, the bean's own code is responsible for starting, committing and rolling back transactions, so it explicitly calls EJBContext.getUserTransaction() to obtain the javax.transaction.UserTransaction handle. Under Container-Managed Transactions (CMT), the container handles all of this transparently via deployment-descriptor attributes, and the bean is actually forbidden from calling getUserTransaction() - doing so throws an IllegalStateException, which rules out options B and C.

questions.question: Struts combine which of these into a unified Framework?
questions.explanation: Apache Struts is an MVC framework built by integrating several Java web technologies: Servlets (the ActionServlet/front controller), JSP (views), and its own custom tag libraries plus a resource-bundle-based message-resources mechanism for internationalized text. Each of (a), (b), (c) names one real ingredient Struts unifies, so the complete and correct answer is that it combines all of them into a single framework.

questions.question: Which locale (i.e., from an internationalization properties file) to use for a user is based on?
questions.explanation: Standard Java/Grails web internationalization resolves the active per-request locale by default from the incoming HTTP request's Accept-Language header - i.e. the user's browser language settings - and then looks up the matching messages_xx.properties file. The named Spring/Groovy configuration file wires up the LocaleResolver and MessageSource beans as infrastructure, but it configures HOW locale is resolved, not the actual per-visitor signal that determines which locale applies.

questions.question: Which of these access specifiers can be used for an interface?
questions.explanation: A top-level Java interface, like a top-level class, may only be declared public or left with default (package-private) access; protected and private are illegal modifiers for a top-level type declaration since they only make sense relative to an enclosing class or member. So among the listed options, only 'public' is a valid access specifier for a top-level interface declaration, making 'All of the mentioned' incorrect. (Nested member interfaces since Java 9 can additionally be private, but that narrower case is not what this question is testing.)

questions.question: In Java, when does method overloading is determined?
questions.explanation: Method overloading is resolved by the compiler using the static (declared) types of the arguments at the call site - this is static/early binding. This contrasts with method overriding, which is resolved at runtime via dynamic dispatch based on the actual object type. 'Coding time' and 'execution time' are not real Java binding phases and exist only to sound similar to 'compile time' and 'run time'.

questions.question: Which component is used to compile, debug and execute java program?
questions.explanation: The Java Development Kit (JDK) is the full toolset for developers: it bundles the javac compiler, a debugger (jdb), and a JRE to run programs, so it alone covers compile, debug AND execute. The JVM is only the runtime engine that executes bytecode, the JRE is the runtime environment (JVM plus libraries) needed only to run programs, and the JIT is a runtime-optimization component inside the JVM - none of these three alone provide compilation and debugging tools.

questions.question: What is true about threading?

options.A: run() method calls start() method and runs the code
options.C: run() method can be called directly without start() method being called
options.D: start() method creates new thread and calls code written in run() method

questions.explanation: Calling start() on a Thread object allocates a new call stack, actually creates a new thread of execution, and that new thread then invokes run() as its entry point. Calling run() directly (option C) is legal and does execute the code, but only synchronously on the current thread, with no new thread spawned - a common beginner mistake that makes C misleading here. Options A and B reverse the real relationship between the two methods; D correctly states that start() is what creates the thread and dispatches to run().

questions.question: Which of the following will ensure the thread will be in running state?
questions.explanation: Strictly, none of these methods guarantees a thread reaches the 'running' state, since final scheduling is always up to the OS/JVM scheduler. Of the choices, yield() is the standard API a programmer uses to influence run-scheduling by voluntarily giving other runnable threads of the same priority a chance to run, and re-enters the runnable pool immediately afterward, making it the closest intended answer. wait() removes the calling thread from execution into a waiting state (the opposite direction); notify() only wakes another thread into runnable, not running, state; and Thread.killThread() is not a real method in the Java API. This question is ambiguously worded, so it is marked low confidence and a disagreement with another solver here would not be surprising.

questions.question: Which option is true about session scope in JSP?

options.A: Objects are accessible only from the page in which they are created
options.B: Objects are accessible only from the pages which are in same session
options.C: Objects are accessible only from the pages which are processing the same request
options.D: Objects are accessible only from the pages which reside in same application

questions.explanation: An object stored with session scope in JSP is bound to the HttpSession and remains accessible from every page the same user visits across multiple requests during that session, until the session ends - that is the entire purpose of session scope. Option (a) instead describes page scope, (c) describes request scope, and (d) describes application scope, each a narrower or broader lifetime than session.

questions.question: Which one is the correct order of phases in JSP life cycle?
questions.explanation: A JSP page is first translated and compiled into a servlet class (Compilation), then jspInit() runs once to set up resources (Initialization), then _jspService() handles each incoming request (Execution), and finally jspDestroy() releases resources when the page is retired (Cleanup). Any option placing Initialization or Cleanup before Compilation, or Cleanup before Execution, is impossible since nothing exists yet at that point to initialize or clean up.

questions.question: Which of these data types is used by operating system to manage the Recursion in Java?
questions.explanation: Each recursive method call pushes a new stack frame (holding local variables, parameters and the return address) onto the thread's call stack, and returning from the call pops that frame off - a strict last-in-first-out discipline that exactly matches how nested calls return. Arrays, queues and trees are not the structure the JVM/OS uses under the hood to track nested method invocations, so they do not fit how recursion is actually implemented.
